articles.title: Anglophone crisis: The lives shattered by Cameroon’s forgotten conflict
articles.summary: More than half a million people have fled their homes since separatist groups demanded independence for Cameroon's English-speaking regions.
articles.body:
Median Bah was just 15 when her life changed forever.

She remembers the date vividly - 7 April 2018. She was ill and confined to her bed.

Armed men stormed her family's compound in Cameroon's Southwest region, one of the country's two English-speaking areas at the centre of a separatist conflict.

Median, now 23, says she was fast asleep when her brother woke her, panicked by the approach of a group of armed men who were shooting indiscriminately.

He escaped through a window. But for Median, fleeing was not so easy.

"Since I was sick, I had no strength to jump through the window with him, so I had to pass through the door," she tells the BBC.

That decision would have devastating consequences.

She says she came face to face with two of the attackers in the backyard, who opened fire at her.

They first shot her in the thigh before firing several more rounds, which severely damaged her face.

"I kept pleading with them not to kill me, that I wasn't feeling well. However, I found myself on the floor," she recalls.

Everything went dark. She lost consciousness and could neither see nor speak.

Median initially thought she was dreaming.

The attack left her with devastating facial injuries. Her jawbone was damaged, most of her teeth destroyed and much of her mouth severely injured.

Over the past eight years, she has undergone at least four reconstructive surgeries in Cameroon, Ghana and India, with more procedures expected next year.

Parts of her face have been reconstructed using tissue taken from other parts of her body.

She also lost the ability to breathe normally through her nose and mouth. She underwent a tracheostomy, a surgical procedure that creates an opening in the neck to allow air into the windpipe.

For eight years, she relied on a tube to breathe. It was only recently removed, allowing her to breathe normally again.

A teenager left with devastating facial injuries, a mother forced to flee her home and a student whose education was disrupted. Nearly a decade of fighting in Cameroon has left countless lives shattered.

The crisis began in October 2016, when lawyers and teachers in Cameroon's English-speaking regions went on strike over the alleged marginalisation of Anglophone communities by the Francophone-dominated government.

They were concerned about the appointment of French-speaking judges and teachers to courts and schools in the English-speaking Northwest and Southwest regions.

Initially, the protest was peaceful, with thousands demanding greater recognition of the English-speaking minority.

But human rights groups accused security forces of using excessive force to suppress the protests. The crackdown, critics say, helped fuel an armed separatist movement.

By 2017, a dozen armed groups had emerged, according to the International Crisis Group, seeking independence for the two English-speaking regions and the creation of a breakaway state known as Ambazonia.

Since then, separatist fighters have engaged in a prolonged and often brutal conflict with government forces.

Rights groups have documented serious abuses by both sides.

Separatist fighters have been accused of targeted killings, kidnappings for ransom, torture and attacks on schools and other public and private facilities.

Government forces, meanwhile, have faced allegations of arbitrary arrests and detention, torture and unlawful killings.

Both sides have denied the accusations, although in some instances they have acknowledged responsibility for abuses.

The violence has devastated communities and forced nearly half a million people from their homes, according to data published by the UN this year.

At least 6,000 people have been killed since the conflict began, according to Human Rights Watch.

The UN refugee agency, UNHCR, says more than 70,000 Cameroonians have sought refuge in neighbouring Nigeria.

Glory Akom, 44, lives with a disability after surviving severe burns in an incident unrelated to the conflict.

The mother-of-two now lives in a camp in Ogoja, a town in Nigeria's south-eastern Cross River state, near the Cameroonian border.

Ogoja hosts about 15,000 refugees across three settlements, Richard Effiong, from the UNHCR, told the BBC.

The UNHCR has provided refugees with brick houses topped with tin roofs.

For many, however, uncertainty remains over when, or whether, they will ever return home.

Glory says her life in Cameroon was far better. She ran a business and was able to provide for her family.

But everything changed when fighting intensified in 2017.

She said soldiers deployed to her area in the Southwest region pursued residents into the bush, forcing them to abandon their homes and flee into Nigeria.

"We were sleeping in the bush, as we were always running," she said.

"If you slept in your house, they could kill you there."

Initially, she settled in a neighbouring village before moving to Ogoja, where she was eventually allocated a permanent home.

Like many other refugees, Glory depends on $67 (£51) monthly cash assistance from UNHCR to support her children, one of who suffers from sickle cell and requires regular medical attention.

The money is barely enough to cover food, medical bills and other necessities, she says.

Her sadness at having to leave home is shared by other Cameroonian refugees in Ogoja who spoke to the BBC.

Maurine Mangha, 21, said she and five other members of her family fled Akwaya in the Southwest region after separatist fighters opened fire during celebrations marking what they described as their independence on 1 October 2017.

"They shot a lot of people, and we had no choice but run into the bush," she tells the BBC.

Maurine had stopped attending school months earlier because of a separatist-imposed education boycott.

The 2017 boycott campaign, which sought to pressure the government, involved threats and attacks against schools and those who defied orders to stay away.

The consequences for children have been severe.

More than 200,000 children are currently out of school in the conflict regions, while nearly 2,500 learning institutions remain non-operational in the two regions, according to the UN's children's agency, Unicef, citing Cameroonian education authorities.

Despite the disruption, Maurine managed to secure a scholarship through a higher education programme for refugees managed by the UNHCR.

She is now studying microbiology at a local polytechnic.

But Maurine says she cannot help thinking about friends who remained in Cameroon.

"I feel very bad for my friends as they did not have the opportunity [to further] their education because of the crisis," she says.

After nearly a decade of fighting, the Cameroonian government wants the separatists to abandon their armed struggle.

In September, the authorities launched a community dialogue initiative aimed at finding grassroots solutions to the conflict.

"It is you, all of us sitting here, who have the capacity today to organise to talk to those boys [separatists], to tell them, the time has come for them to leave," Prime Minister Joseph Dion Ngute said during the launch in Buea, capital of the Southwest region.

He repeated a similar message in Bamenda, the main city in the Northwest region and one of the epicentres of the conflict.

At both events, nearly 60 people described as former separatist fighters were presented as having abandoned the armed struggle and surrendered to the state.

A similar initiative in 2019 failed to end the fighting.

As of November 2026, almost 1,500 former separatist fighters were undergoing rehabilitation at Disarmament, Demobilisation and Reintegration (DDR) centres in the two English-speaking regions, a Cameroonian official from the agency overseeing the programme told the BBC.

"A lot of Amba boys [separatist fighters] have been killed, others have surrendered, and many of them have abandoned the ideology of independence," says Clovis Naseri, a former separatist commander.

Clovis spent about two years with the White Tigers of Ribbons, an armed group operating in the Southwest region, before abandoning the group in 2019.

He was subsequently admitted to a reintegration centre, where he underwent rehabilitation for several years.

He is now a vocal critic of the separatist movement and advocates peace and national unity.

Despite defections and government efforts to encourage fighters to surrender, separatist groups continue to carry out attacks across the two regions.

Some analysts argue that the conflict has persisted for so long partly because of the government's failure to address the grievances that triggered it.

Roland Fru, a researcher on the Anglophone crisis, says the authorities are yet to demonstrate a clear understanding of the issues driving the conflict.

"I've not heard even once, the government explain things in such a way that helps me understand that they even understand the problem," he says.

The BBC contacted several government officials for comment but did not receive a response.

Cameroonian authorities have frequently rejected criticism of their handling of the crisis.

Last November, President Paul Biya said the reconstruction efforts, supported by international partners, were helping restore normality in the affected regions.

"These efforts will continue steadily," he said during his swearing-in ceremony, while praising security forces for their "effective actions" and "professionalism" in improving the situation.

For survivors such as Median, Glory and Maurine, however, lasting peace may remain elusive until the fighting comes to a permanent end.

As they try to rebuild their lives and hold on to hope, Median, who still lives in Cameroon, says she remains grateful to have survived.

"I have defeated death," she says confidently. "I don't think there's anything that can stop me."

articles.title: Van Hollen: Abrego Garcia leaving US, ‘will be safe’ amid self-deportation reports
articles.summary: Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose wrongful deportation became a flashpoint in the debate over President Trump’s immigration crackdown, self-deported Tuesday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed. ABC News reported Abrego Garcia boarded a flight from a Washington, D.C.-area airport to Madrid, Spain. His departure came as he was facing deportation to one of several…
articles.body:
Salvadoran migrant Kilmar Abrego Garcia , whose wrongful deportation became a flashpoint in the debate over President Trump’s immigration crackdown, self-deported Tuesday, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed.

ABC News reported Abrego Garcia boarded a flight from a Washington, D.C.-area airport to Madrid, Spain. His departure came as he was facing deportation to one of several African countries proposed by the Department of Homeland Security.

Van Hollen, who met with Abrego Garcia in El Salvador’s mega-prison , CECOT , last year, said in a statement to The Hill that “Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity” after the Trump administration “wanted to leave Kilmar Abrego Garcia to rot in a Salvadoran gulag.”

He added he was “relieved” Abrego Garcia “will be safe.”

“While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation,” Van Hollen said.

Abrego Garcia was expected to appear for a hearing in his immigration case last month before U.S. District Judge Paula Xinis canceled it, ABC News reported.

Abrego Garcia had lived in Maryland for years until he was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported shortly after. A 2019 court order barred his deportation back to El Salvador due to dangers he and his family faced from a Salvadoran gang.

He was allowed back into the U.S. without residency status and under Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) supervision.

The Trump administration accused Abrego Garcia of being a member of the criminal gang MS-13, something the Salvadoran man has denied. Former Attorney General Pam Bondi claimed on Fox News in April 2025 that “all these liberal reporters, they keep calling him a Maryland man. He’s not a Maryland man. He’s part of foreign terrorist organization.”

The Supreme Court upheld a ruling requiring the White House to “facilitate” Abrego Garcia’s return to the U.S. He came back to the U.S. in June, but the Department of Justice (DOJ) later filed an indictment against him on human smuggling charges in connection with a 2022 traffic stop in Tennessee.

Xinis ordered Abrego Garcia’s release from ICE custody while he awaited trial and forbade the agency from detaining him again.

In May, a federal judge dismissed the Justice Department’s (DOJ) indictment against him, which it swiftly appealed. In his decision, U.S. District Court Judge Waverly Crenshaw had accused the indictment of being vindictive .

The DOJ in August asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit to reinstate the charges against Abrego Garcia, denying Crenshaw’s characterization of the criminal proceedings and calling his order “erroneous at every step.”

articles.title: A federal grand jury indicts Thomas Markle on child sex abuse material charges
articles.summary: LOS ANGELES — A federal grand jury in Los Angeles on Tuesday indicted the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, on charges that he kept child sexual abuse material — including photos where Markle himself was pictured with prepubescent children, according to prosecutors.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — A federal grand jury in Los Angeles on Tuesday indicted the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, on charges that he kept child sexual abuse material — including photos where Markle himself was pictured with prepubescent children, according to prosecutors. If convicted, Thomas Wayne Markle, 82, could be sentenced to up to 40 years in prison, according to a statement shared by top Los Angeles federal prosecutor Bill Essayli. He has previously denied any wrongdoing. Markle was arrested in early November after federal officials say they found dozens of illicit images, including film negatives, slides and books depicting suspected child abuse, in a storage facility in Los Angeles. Court filings also allege Markle possessed similar material in the Philippines, where he has a home and where some of the lewd photos of the children appear to have been taken. Markle himself was identified by a witness in at least two photos with a nude, prepubescent girl, according to the indictment. Markle is in jail in Florida, where he was arrested Nov. 6 at a senior living facility, but he will be transferred to Los Angeles in the coming weeks, Essayli’s office wrote. Markle moved to the United States from the Philippines after having a stroke this year that resulted in his left leg being amputated. He was initially granted bond after his arrest but was detained again days later when he attempted to cut his ankle monitor off in the middle of the night. The indictment comes shortly after a judge ruled Markle was mentally sound enough to stand trial based on an analysis conducted by an expert psychiatrist. The federal public defender representing Markle didn’t immediately respond to an emailed request for comment Tuesday afternoon, but Markle previously denied any wrongdoing in his 90-minute competency interview in mid-November, according to a report filed by the psychiatrist who conducted the interview. “Why I am here. What have I done?” the psychiatrist quoted him as saying. “I don’t have any child porn. I have no pictures of naked kids.” The psychiatrist ultimately said in her report that Markle understands the charges against him and can assist his lawyer — two key points in any competency determination. The expert said he was “malingering,” or exaggerating, at times in his responses during the interview. Meanwhile, in the Philippines, Markle is under investigation for possession and intent to distribute illegal child abuse images, Brig. Gen. Allen Rae Co said in a written statement.

articles.title: What is the Fifth Amendment, and why is Trump urging Jensen Huang not to invoke it
articles.summary: US president Donald Trump has urged Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to tell the truth when he faces congressional questioning next week.
articles.body: US president Donald Trump has urged Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to tell the truth when he faces congressional questioning next week. Adding that he does not believe the chipmaker’s head needs to invoke the Fifth Amendment over his alleged links to a woman suspected of having connections to Chinese intelligence.Trump also said he was open to granting Huang a presidential pardon if necessary, but did not think such a step would be required.Asked in an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday whether he would consider pardoning Huang over potential crimes, Trump said, “It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary.”“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said, adding that he wanted Huang to “just tell the truth”.Trump said he had always found Huang to be “100% aboveboard” and described him as a “very smart person”, while acknowledging that the Nvidia chief’s lawyers would have to advise him on how to approach the questioning.What is the Fifth Amendment?The Fifth Amendment to the US Constitution protects individuals from being compelled to give testimony that could incriminate them in a criminal case.The protection is commonly known as the right against self-incrimination. When a person refuses to answer a question on this basis, the act is often described as “pleading the Fifth”.The amendment forms part of the Bill of Rights, ratified in 1791, and also includes protections against double jeopardy, guarantees of due process and limits on the government’s power to take private property without just compensation.Invoking the Fifth Amendment is a constitutional right and does not, by itself, establish guilt, but it does create a sense of doubt surrounding the innocence. Whether Huang chooses to invoke it during congressional questioning would be a decision made with advice from his lawyers.Why is Jensen Huang facing scrutiny?Huang is expected to testify before US lawmakers in relation to questions about Nvidia’s business dealings with China and compliance with American export restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips.The scrutiny has also centred on Huang’s relationship with a Chinese woman suspected by US intelligence officials of having links to Chinese intelligence. Huang has acknowledged having an affair with the woman.Lawmakers are also expected to examine allegations that Nvidia chips may have been diverted to Chinese AI companies through third countries, potentially circumventing US export controls.According to CNN, Huang is scheduled to testify behind closed doors before a US Senate committee on Tuesday next week, followed by a public hearing on Friday.The hearings are expected to focus on Nvidia’s export practices and the national security implications of its business dealings with China.Nvidia’s board has also reinstated Huang as chief executive, following his removal from the position less than two weeks earlier. articles.title: Former VP Al Gore returning to his roots to become new owner of Tennessee newsaper
articles.summary: Former Vice President Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town.
articles.body: Former Vice President Al Gore, who started his career as a journalist, is returning to the industry as a newspaper owner in his Tennessee town. The Lake family, which has operated the Carthage Courier for five decades, said Tuesday it will sell the paper to Gore in the coming weeks. The weekly paper serves Smith County in central Tennessee, which has roughly 20,000 residents and sits about 55 miles east of Nashville. As the beleaguered news industry struggles with newspaper closures and growing news deserts, Gore characterized the purchase as a move that preserves an independent local voice in Carthage and Smith County. “Having spent my early years as a military reporter in Vietnam and later at the (Nashville) Tennessean, I am a firm believer that a free, independent local press is irreplaceable for the enduring health of our community,” Gore said in a statement. Terms of the sale weren’t disclosed, and it wasn’t clear how involved Gore, 78, will be in the paper’s operations. His office and the outlet wouldn’t answer questions Tuesday or provide additional details. The Courier’s announcement omitted Gore’s political resume, presenting him simply as a local man buying his small town’s paper to keep it locally owned. Before entering politics, Gore spent six months as a military reporter in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam War. He returned to Tennessee and worked for a few years as an investigative reporter at The Tennessean before running for Congress in 1976. Gore, a Democrat, represented Tennessee in both chambers of Congress, served as President Bill Clinton’s vice president from 1993 to 2001, and ran for president twice. After losing the 2000 presidential election to George W. Bush, he went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize for his climate activism and an Academy Award for the documentary, “An Inconvenient Truth.” The Courier’s website notes that it covered the early political pursuits of Gore’s father, Albert Gore Sr., who represented the state in the U.S. House and Senate. Tim Franklin, chair of local news at Northwestern University’s Medill School of Journalism, Media, Integrated Marketing Communications, said Carthage residents may have “some healthy skepticism” about a politician owning the paper. “But I would be surprised if the Carthage Courier becomes a mouthpiece for the Democratic Party,” he said. Franklin wondered if the former vice president might write a column, and if the publication would remain narrowly focused on local news. Gore is far from the first politician to purchase or own a newspaper. Throughout the 1900s, several senators, governors and even a U.S. president, Warren Harding, had local papers in their business portfolios. More recently, consumer advocate Ralph Nader, one of Gore’s former political rivals, helped launch a local newspaper in Winsted, Connecticut, in 2023 that was purchased months later by a national media company.

articles.title: He’s remained jailed in Japan despite an overturned conviction. His family in the US fears for his life
articles.summary: Despite no charge against him, Chris Payne remains behind bars, a punishment the now 34-year-old described to CNN as “purgatory.”
articles.body: Christopher Payne’s dream was to build a life in Japan. As a 12-year-old in Indiana, he fell in love with the country through anime, spending hours watching Pokémon on YouTube. He taught himself Japanese and eventually became fluent. In 2013, he started living in Japan, first to teach English and then to work for one of Japan’s biggest internet companies. But in 2021, his dreams were dashed. He was arrested for sexual assault—a crime he maintains he didn’t commit—and sentenced to eight years in prison for a conviction that has since been overturned. A high court ordered a retrial, but no date has been set. Despite no charge against him, Payne remains behind bars, a punishment the now 34-year-old described to CNN as “purgatory.” “Instead of counting down the days until I’m released, like a guilty person would, I’m tallying the days I’ve spent behind bars,” he said in an interview from jail. Lawyers, activists and Payne’s loved ones say his case is an example of Japan’s “hostage justice,” a term referring to the detention of suspects without charge for far longer than the law in other countries would allow, often for days, if not weeks. When CNN visited Payne in late October at a prison in Chiba, east of Tokyo, the toll of his detention was difficult to ignore. He was coughing up blood and repeatedly lost his train of thought, stopping mid-sentence as he struggled to remember what he had been saying. At times, his body convulsed. He also complained of severe headaches. By the end of our meeting, he was so weak that he had to be taken away in a wheelchair. “I might not have much more fight in me,” he said. An overturned conviction Payne’s saga began in July 2018, years before his arrest, when a woman was sexually assaulted in Ichikawa in Chiba prefecture, where Payne lived. According to Payne’s lawyers, a woman told police she had been attacked while walking home at night by a masked man. He spoke Japanese without an accent and forced the woman to perform oral sex. The attacker fled and the victim returned home, where she rinsed her mouth before contacting police. Investigators were left with only trace amounts of DNA, Payne’s lawyers told CNN. Then, in an unrelated incident nearly two years later, Payne was detained after falling asleep drunk in the doorway of a stranger’s home. The resident didn’t press charges and Payne was released 24 hours later, but he consented to a voluntary DNA swab - a decision that would forever alter his life, his lawyers added. In November 2021, police arrested him after a database search found his DNA was “consistent” with trace evidence recovered from the 2018 assault, his attorneys said. Payne has repeatedly denied the allegations since and his defense team, unconvinced by the forensic evidence, sent the raw DNA data to be independently examined by a forensic DNA consultant in the United States. The expert found that the DNA files from the crime scene appeared to have been edited in a way that made them more closely resemble Payne’s DNA, according to his lawyers. The high court eventually overturned his conviction in December 2025 and ordered a retrial, after the findings raised serious questions about the reliability of the evidence that had helped put Payne behind bars. Under Japan’s criminal justice system, Payne remains behind bars and has been denied bail, despite his team’s repeated requests. “The reason (given) was (the) risk of destroying evidence. But we think it’s impossible for Chris to destroy DNA evidence,” one of his lawyers, Kiyomi Tsunogae, said in a press conference. “That’s the only evidence they have.” Since December last year, Payne says he has repeatedly coughed up blood. Despite numerous requests for a thorough medical examination, he says the only significant test he has received is a blood test. “It showed I wasn’t anemic, so they said I’m probably not experiencing internal bleeding and therefore, it’s not a serious problem,” Payne told CNN. Payne’s lawyers and supporters say the court has rejected repeated requests for a proper medical examination. Prosecutors and the Ministry of Justice declined to comment directly on the reasons for Payne’s continued detention or allegations of DNA from the crime scene being edited. Prosecutors maintained Payne is receiving appropriate medical care. ‘I can’t wait to just hug him’ From the other side of the world, Payne’s mother Ronda is waging her own battle to clear her son’s name and bring him home. Speaking to CNN from her home in northwest Indiana, Ronda said she’s sent hundreds of emails and letters to local representatives and the US Embassy, pleading for help. But given her son’s case falls outside US legal jurisdiction, there’s been little progress, she said. Inside her home, the absence of her son is impossible to miss. His bedroom appears frozen in time, with photos from his younger years still lining the walls. His bed is piled with Christmas and birthday presents he has never had the chance to open. Ronda remembers her son as a boy who was always ambitious. He loved sports, but also played piano and drew. More than anything, she said, he had a way of making people laugh. His goofy personality could light up any room. She also described him as one of the strongest men she knows. “Him staying alive, he’s fighting for our family. And I thank him. I can’t wait to just hug him and tell him how proud I am of him,” she told CNN. But as the legal fight continues, Payne’s defense team and supporters are increasingly worried that Payne may not be well enough to see it through. Kouta Handa, the father of Payne’s ex-girlfriend and one of his biggest supporters, has been visiting him regularly since his arrest five years ago, watching Payne’s condition slowly deteriorate. “I’m really worried. And if this situation continues, he might die in the detention center,” he told CNN. Although Payne and Handa’s daughter separated amicably months before Payne’s arrest, Handa has continued to stand by him. “I love him. I and my wife think of him like our own son,” he said. Handa says he feels sorry for Payne in Japan’s judicial system, which has long faced international scrutiny over its detention practices, interrogation methods and extraordinarily high conviction rate. “I as a Japanese I feel very sorry for him because the Japanese judicial system made a serious mistake. And due to that mistake, Chris is suffering from very harsh conditions for more than five years,” he said. The US State Department said Embassy staff have regularly visited Payne to verify he is receiving “fair, transparent, and humane treatment, with the most recent visit on October 27. “We remain in contact with Mr. Payne and his family and will continue to stay closely engaged in his case,” a State Department spokesperson said. A system under scrutiny Payne’s experience is the among the latest cases to bring international attention to the way people suspected of crimes are treated in Japan – in addition to the cases of ex-Nissan chief Carlos Ghosn, who fled house arrest in 2019 while awaiting trial, and Iwao Hakamata, the world’s longest-serving death row prisoner who was exonerated in 2024. Japan’s Ministry of Justice has repeatedly rejected allegations of “hostage justice,” saying it respects the rights of the accused. But the high conviction rate and scale of pre-indictment detention continues to raise alarm by legal scholars and activists. Figures released by the Ministry of Justice show that in 2025, of 67,052 requests by prosecutors to extend detention, judges rejected just 200. Hiroshi Ichikawa, a former prosecutor who is now a defense lawyer, told CNN that Japan’s system of pretrial detention effectively presumes defendants guilty before they have had their day in court. “Prosecutors and judges publicly claim to uphold the presumption of innocence. But their actions suggest the opposite,” said Ichikawa, who is not involved in Payne’s case. Japan’s conviction rate stands at over 99%, according to its Ministry of Justice. It’s heavily reliant on confessions and retrials are rare. Human rights experts, former prosecutors and defense lawyers have questioned what that figure says about the fairness of the system, pointing to prosecutorial practices they argue can pressure suspects into confessing and make it difficult to secure an acquittal. Ichikawa also said the use of bail is another way the system puts pressure on defendants. Judges routinely oppose bail for those who deny the charges, he said, and they “almost always side with the prosecution.” “The result is that the more insistently an innocent person maintains their innocence, the longer they can be kept behind bars. Some eventually feel they have no choice but to admit to a crime they did not commit just to get out of detention.” As Payne continues to wait behind bars for his case to proceed through the justice system, his loved ones fear not only that he may not return home, but what’s left when he finally does. “I don’t know what’s next. I don’t know how he’s going to do. I’m often afraid of how he is gonna live when he comes home because he’s been in isolation,” Ronda said through tears.

articles.title: Miss Universe crowns winner after another turbulent year for world’s biggest pageant
articles.summary: Puerto Rico’s Jennifer Barreto won Miss Universe 2026 on home soil at Tuesday night’s finale in San Juan.
articles.body: Jennifer Barreto of Puerto Rico was crowned Miss Universe 2026 on home soil, capping off another tumultuous 12 months for the scandal-plagued pageant. With last year’s vote-rigging allegations casting a long shadow over the annual contest, the 27-year-old social worker triumphed over 115 other finalists — a number significantly depleted by late withdrawals due to visa issues and a fractious business dispute — at Tuesday’s grand finale in San Juan, the self-governing US territory’s capital city. Barreto is the first married woman and first mother to win Miss Universe since organizers lifted its controversial ban on contestants who have ever wed, or given birth, three years ago. Tuesday evening’s pageant opened with an elimination round, based on judges’ scores from various preliminary contests. Thirty remaining contestants then participated in an on-stage swimwear contest, with 12 advancing to an evening gown parade. The final five then faced judges’ questions on topics including the relevance of the Miss Universe pageant and what the world needs from its leaders. Asked which human value we should “never lose” amid the growth of artificial intelligence, Barreto said, in Spanish, that the “best thing is to use it responsibly,” adding: “If artificial intelligence puts our values at risk, then they were never values. Values are found in the consistency between what we say and what we do, especially when upholding those things becomes difficult.” While the glitzy finale proved hiccup-free, many of this year’s controversies unfolded in the weeks and months leading up to the event. Beauty queens from Nepal and five African countries, including first-time participants South Sudan and the Republic of Congo, were forced to drop out due to difficulties or delays obtaining US visas. Elsewhere, an ongoing contractual dispute between the Miss Universe Organization and Thai businessman Nawat Itsaragrisil, who operates qualifying pageants in six Southeast Asian countries, meant that delegates from Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam were all absent from the final. Earlier, in May, organizers of Miss Universe France withdrew their delegate in protest at 2025’s final, which became embroiled in claims of vote-rigging and favoritism. (The Miss Universe Organization later formed a selection committee to appoint an alternative Miss France, Garance Authié, who advanced to Tuesday’s Top 12.) Last year, three days before the finale, judge Omar Harfouch resigned over his belief that results had been pre-scripted by an unofficial “impromptu jury.” Harfouch also alleged that winner Miss Mexico, Fátima Bosch — who was in attendance Tuesday to crown her successor on stage — had triumphed because of her father’s alleged business ties to Miss Universe’s co-owner, Raúl Rocha Cantú. The controversial Mexican businessman and the Miss Universe Organization have consistently denied the allegations. But questions over the judging process hung over this year’s contest, with the jury only unveiled a day before the finale. It has now been three years since independent auditor Ernst & Young (which previously handed hosts the results in a sealed envelope) was last involved in the pageant. Itsaragrisil, the Thai pageant director, was among those calling for reform. “I would like contestants to know who will judge them, how the judges are selected, how scores are verified and how conflicts of interest are handled,” he told CNN via text message, prior to the competition. He hopes his six withdrawn Southeast Asian delegates can instead participate next year. Miss Universe did not respond to CNN’s request for comment on this year’s judging process or its dispute with Itsaragrisil ahead of the pageant. While the contest is no longer a fixture on American network TV, it continues to prove popular among Latino communities, with Telemundo reporting growing audience numbers for its annual broadcast. The Spanish-language screening of 2025’s finale was viewed by 2.6 million people, the broadcaster said, up from 2.1 million the previous year. Only the US and Venezuela have won more Miss Universe titles than Puerto Rico, which now has six. The US territory was hosting the final for the fourth time in the pageant’s 75-year history, having previously done so in 1972, 2001 — when Puerto Rican Denise Quiñones also won on home soil — and 2002. On a successful evening for Latin American contestants, Melissa Núñez of the Dominican Republic and Clara Vegas of Venezuela were named first and second runners-up, respectively. The Miss Universe Organization ended its divisive ban on pregnant women, mothers and contestants who are — or ever have been — married in light of growing calls for the pageant to modernize. In 2023, organizers also ended a longstanding ban on over-28s. A series of preliminary rounds took place ahead of Tuesday’s finale, including closed-door interviews and the national costume contest. During the latter, some boos were heard as Miss Israel, Danielle Yablonka, walked down the runway in a cape bearing the word “peace” in English, Hebrew and Arabic.

articles.title: How Ukraine is using AI to track and destroy Russian forces
articles.summary: The kinetic conflict underway in eastern Ukraine has for long demonstrated how wars in the future will be fought.
articles.body: The kinetic conflict underway in eastern Ukraine has for long demonstrated how wars in the future will be fought. The conflict, which is nearing the five-year mark, has upended the long-held view that wars of the 21st century will be short but intense affairs. The conflict has also demonstrated how unmanned systems in air, land and sea will shape conflicts that are yet to come. One important lesson from this conflict is how to carefully form and curate an ever-developing combat picture, which is sourced from thousands of data collection points, such as drones, sensors and humans alike. As is the case everywhere else in combat too, information is king. Correct and timely information is key to winning engagements, for centuries generals and tacticians alike have been hampered by the fog of war. In modern conflict with resources available from human intelligence to satellites high up in space, this fog has greatly reduced, and with new combat management systems, ever-increasing clarity is available to decision makers at all levels.Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system has evolved from a digital mapping tool into an integrated network connecting reconnaissance, intelligence and military operations. Developed in 2016 by the volunteer organisation Aerorozvidka, which was experimenting with drones and digital reconnaissance in eastern Ukraine, DELTA was designed to give commanders a common operational picture by combining information from multiple sources.According to the Zurich based Swiss Center for Security Studies, the system received support through the NATO-Ukraine Command, Control, Communications and Computers Trust Fund and was first deployed on a major scale during the defence of Kyiv in February-March 2022. Ukrainian units used it to share information on Russian troop movements, drone video feeds, satellite imagery, surveillance camera footage and intelligence from civilian sources. Starlink connectivity enabled frontline units to transmit information to headquarters, allowing commanders to monitor developments and coordinate responses.DELTA has since expanded beyond digital mapping, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), its applications include mission control for scheduling and coordinating drone missions, Vezha for streaming and analysing UAV footage, and Delta Tube for accessing live video feeds. Its integration with the Avengers artificial intelligence platform allows the analysis of multiple drone feeds and the identification and classification of objects.The French Institute of International Relations (IFRI), in a 2026 study, notes that DELTA received formal authorisation from Ukraine’s defence ministry in 2023, helping it develop into a wider digital ecosystem. Its components now include monitor for situational awareness, target Hub for target management and element for encrypted communications. The system is intended to process information from drones, satellites, radar, acoustic sensors and intelligence units, helping commanders prioritise targets and coordinate strikes.An Atlantic Council study also published in 2026 cited claims that integrating intelligence through DELTA had reduced the time between target detection and engagement from around 72 hours to approximately two minutes. The figure is an attributed operational claim and should not be treated as a universal measure. DELTA has also been tested with Poland’s TOPAZ artillery command system and during NATO’s CWIX interoperability exercises in 2024.Alongside DELTA, Ukraine is developing ODIN, an artificial intelligence-based system created by officers from its military institute of telecommunications and information technologies. Presented at the NATO TIDE Hackathon in March 2026, the prototype combines intelligence from different sources, prioritises targets and generates possible courses of action, including kinetic, non-kinetic and cyber options.However, there is no independent evidence that ODIN has been widely deployed or integrated with DELTA. While DELTA has become an established part of Ukraine’s digital battlefield architecture, ODIN remains at the prototype stage. Together, the developments underline Ukraine’s effort to connect sensors, intelligence, command systems and weapons into a network that can shorten the time between detecting an enemy and engaging it.

articles.title: Days after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized for disruption in Outlook services globally, company declares 'Code Red' for its engineers; internal memo says ...
articles.summary: Days after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologised for a major outage that disrupted Outlook and other Microsoft 265 services across the world,
articles.body: Days after Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologised for a major outage that disrupted Outlook and other Microsoft 265 services across the world, the company has declared ‘Code Red’ initiative which is aimed at overhauling its engineering, incident response and service recovery processes, as per the internal memos reviewed by Reuters. This move from Microsoft comes after the November 12-13 outage which impacted governments, businesses and consumers across multiple countries, including Australia, Japan and the United States. The service disruption affected Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, Copilot and other Microsoft 365 services, raising fresh concerns about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure. Microsoft also said that the incident was not caused by cyberattack or AI-related activity. Instead, the company attributed the outrage to an undetected Windows scalability defect which was introduced un July.‘Most customer-impacting incident’ in Exchange Online historyAccording to an internal memo cited by Reuters, M365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as the most customer-impacting incident in the history of Exchange Online. "Never before had so many customers been without email for so long," Henderson reportedly told employees, emphasising that the Code Red designation represents the highest-priority work across the team.The outage lasted nearly 24 hours and affected several core Microsoft cloud services, disrupting communications for enterprises, government agencies and other organisations that rely on Microsoft 365.Engineers battled ‘fog of war’ during outageIn a separate memo on Monday, Amanda Silver, a corporate vice president overseeing M365 Core and Work IQ, said engineers worked through a “fog of war.” Despite deploying top engineers, responders exchanged more than 11,000 messages across 11 Teams chats and struggled to keep a clear picture of hypotheses and decisions, because diagnostic data was scattered across fragmented internal tracking systems.Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures, according to Silver’s memo.Microsoft targets one-hour global recoveryAs part of the Code Red effort, Microsoft has launched several high-priority workstreams focused on load shedding, geographic traffic partitioning and faster recovery mechanisms.The company has reportedly set an ambitious goal of resolving future global incidents within one hour. Microsoft also plans to use AI agents to help engineers analyse system health data and diagnose issues more quickly during outages.Henderson is expected to conduct daily reviews with the leadership team overseeing Substrate, the engineering platform that underpins many Microsoft 365 services, alongside weekly progress assessments.Internal review exposes broader operational weaknessesReuters reported that Henderson's review of the outage identified wider organisational and structural issues beyond the specific software defect that triggered the failure. In a separate memo reviewed by the news agency, Henderson said urgent patches for Microsoft 365 Core services were being deployed too slowly across global infrastructure.He reportedly cited a separate recent incident in which a critical production fix required five to six days to achieve worldwide deployment. According to the memo, Microsoft aims to reduce the time between detecting urgent security issues and safely deploying fixes globally to just one hour. "Unfortunately, all the work we have done over the years was not sufficient to protect us on Thursday," Henderson wrote, according to Reuters.Satya Nadella on Microsoft outageMicrosoft should have caught the software bug that took Outlook offline last week and had safeguards to contain the disruption, chief executive Satya Nadella has said. In an interview with CNBC’s Jim Cramer, Nadella said that the flaw surfaced only under a particular pattern of traffic. “Of course, we should have done the testing before,” he said. The outage disrupted email at businesses that rely on Outlook for day-to-day communication. Nadella said Microsoft should have designed its systems so that a failure in one part of the service could be isolated before it spread globally.He also raised a broader problem for companies running older infrastructure. AI tools can help engineers identify software flaws and develop fixes faster, but each fix still has to be tested and installed. More frequent updates, he said, can make existing systems less stable. His comments pointed to a trade-off for software providers as they accelerate the release of patches while keeping widely used services online. "Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable," Nadella said. "I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet."Fearless legend or grounded realist? Rate yourself on 11 categories in the Great Indian Confidence Survey – find out in 3–6 min

articles.title: Pakistan rejoices as country’s first astronaut enters orbit
articles.summary: Zeeshan Ali makes history as the first foreign national to board China’s space station
articles.body:
The first person from Pakistan to go into orbit has made history as the first foreign astronaut to board China’s Tiangong space station.

Muhammad Zeeshan Ali docked at the space station in the early hours of Wednesday after taking off from China’s Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in northwest China on board a Chinese-made rocket.

Ali, 40, will stay in space for five to 10 days, shorter than the usual six-month stints Chinese astronauts serve.

“I’m not flying for myself. I carry the name of Pakistan on my shoulder,” Ali told reporters on Tuesday.

While most of the infrastructure behind Ali’s space trip is Chinese, he has trained for months in China, including by learning Chinese, to make the trip happen.

“This is not just one astronaut’s journey, but the journey of 240 million Pakistanis. It is the journey of our younger generation, our scientists and our dreams,” Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said in a post on X.

“This is living proof of the ironclad friendship between Pakistan and China. We are grateful to our brother country, China, for making Pakistan part of this historic mission.”

Chinese President Xi Jinping said the joint mission with astronauts from China and Pakistan is “a vivid embodiment of the deep-rooted friendship between the two countries”.

This is a big diplomatic moment for China. Beijing is eager to show the world that the Tiangong space station has the potential to become an international research platform rather than an exclusive Chinese facility.

China has been ramping up its space industry and aims to put a Chinese astronaut on the moon by 2030. The US aims to do the same in 2028, for the first time since the 1972 Apollo 17 flight.

China plans to establish a ‌research ‌base on the moon by 2035 with Russia.

Both Beijing and Washington insist their presence in space is entirely peaceful, but the US has warned that China could seek to dominate resource-rich areas of the moon.

articles.title: Countries that thrive on global cooperation must help sustain it
articles.summary: Prosperous small states like Qatar should combine their diplomatic and economic resources to advance global stability.
articles.body:
“For thriving states, international peace and stability are not a luxury. They are the foundation of our national stories.”

Qatar’s Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani made this point at the Oxford Union earlier this month. For countries such as Qatar, prosperity rests on connections extending far beyond their borders. Energy exports, shipping routes and overseas investments depend on international predictability. Their security policy has to reflect that.

The meeting of the presidents of the United States, China and Russia – Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin – in Shenzhen on November 19 brought the problem into focus. Their declaration covered nuclear risks, energy supplies and reform of the United Nations. These are matters that affect every country. A few powers retain disproportionate influence over the outcome.

Dialogue among these powers is welcome. We should, however, have no illusions that their willingness to sit together signals the end of their competition. They can reach agreements while continuing to contest influence and access to resources. For countries outside the room, the consequences may arrive through a disrupted shipping route, a new restriction on trade or a security decision they had no part in making.

The prime minister’s concept of thriving states offers a way to think about their response. He described agile, stable and prosperous countries that have built influence beyond their size. Economic strength, adaptable institutions and trusted relationships give them room to act. Their exposure to decisions taken elsewhere gives them a reason to act together. Economic importance is no guarantee of security.

Thriving states can also help bridge the gaps between competing great powers. By maintaining diplomatic and economic ties with all sides, they can keep channels open when relations deteriorate. This gives them room to facilitate dialogue, support conflict resolution and identify areas where rivals still have an interest in cooperating.

The familiar classifications are of limited help here. The Global North and the Global South tell us little about which countries can work together on a particular problem. Developed and developing say something about economic conditions, but much less about diplomatic reach or the ability to support a peace process. A country may be small in population and still possess capabilities that larger states need.

Negotiations still have to take place. Aid needs access, ceasefires need monitoring, and agreements need someone to keep working on them after the announcement. Thriving states should take greater responsibility for this work. Their diplomatic access and financial resources are increasingly necessary to sustain functions that international institutions struggle to perform consistently.

Qatar is already doing this through its mediation between Washington and Tehran and its work on implementing the Gaza agreement. The limits of these efforts are visible. Agreements are violated, talks stall and violence continues. Maintaining a channel nevertheless preserves the possibility of a negotiated outcome. That channel has to survive setbacks if it is to be useful when an opening appears.

At Oxford, the prime minister pointed to Qatar’s cooperation with Norway and Switzerland on the situation in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Such partnerships bring different relationships and experience to mediation. They offer a practical basis for cooperation among states that share an interest in a settlement, even when their wider foreign policies differ.

Regional organisations remain essential. In eastern DRC, Qatari facilitation of negotiations between the Congolese government and the AFC/M23 rebel alliance has worked alongside efforts by the African Union, the US and Switzerland. Continued fighting and limited implementation show how much remains to be done. Thriving states should strengthen these partnerships and support the regional institutions involved.

The work also requires money and a longer view of what makes peace last. Preliminary OECD figures put Qatar’s official development assistance in 2025 at more than $900m. Restoring services, supporting institutions and creating economic opportunities are all critical for the settlement of conflicts. People need to see that an agreement changes something in their lives.

Commercial investment matters for a related reason. A 2025 Federal Reserve staff study documented how foreign direct investment is fragmenting along ideological and geographical lines. A government seeking finance for infrastructure or technology increasingly has to consider the strategic dependencies that may accompany it. Control of a port or a critical supply chain can give an outside power influence well beyond the original investment.

Thriving states have an opportunity to offer investment with fewer demands for geopolitical alignment. For a country with limited coercive reach and an economy dependent on international exchange, keeping markets open may be more valuable than drawing other countries into an exclusive sphere of influence. The benefit to recipients is greater choice over both their economic partners and their foreign policy.

That difference has to be demonstrated. Thriving states have interests, and their investments also generate influence.

The next step is to organise sustained cooperation among willing thriving states. Their economies are already connected through trade and investment. Their diplomatic cooperation should acquire comparable depth. A standing partnership would allow them to combine capabilities around particular problems while retaining their own priorities. Agreement on every international dispute is an unrealistic condition for useful work.

The same layered and networked approach I have advocated for Gulf security applies here: different partners undertake different tasks, and their efforts need to connect. In a peace process, one country may have access to the parties while another can support monitoring or implementation. Governments should agree how to bring those contributions together before the next crisis demands them.

Development agencies should pool resources for implementing agreements, with priorities established in consultation with local institutions and affected communities. Commercial investors can support recovery where viable opportunities exist. Financing and implementation arrangements should be prepared during negotiations, so that a signed agreement is followed by work people can see. Leaving those questions until later risks losing the opening that diplomacy has created.

The partnership should support the UN and regional organisations with funding, expertise and coordinated diplomacy. It will also need consistency. Sovereignty and civilian protection must matter when a partner violates them. Countries asking for a greater role in international security should be prepared to defend the principles that make their own prosperity possible. And we saw this very clearly when Qatar defended itself against Iranian aggression earlier this year.

Shenzhen is a reminder that major powers will continue to negotiate over the shape of the international order. Thriving states have their own resources and interests to bring to that discussion. They should begin by organising the work they already do and committing to sustain it together. Acting separately gives them less influence than their combined capabilities should permit.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

articles.title: Saudi-led coalition intercepts Houthi attacks after Hodeidah strike
articles.summary: The escalation comes after the Yemeni rebel group threatened to attack the kingdom’s Red Sea ports in retaliation.
articles.body:
Saudi Arabia says its air defences have intercepted several drones launched by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, a day after the Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government carried out an air strike on the rebel-held port city of Hodeidah.

The coalition’s spokesman Turki Al-Maliki said that Saudi air defence systems destroyed four drones in Ras Tanura in Saudi Arabia’s east on Wednesday morning, adding that fragments fell due to the interception, with no casualties reported in the initial assessment.

Al-Maliki said earlier that three drones were also shot down in the Eastern province.

The interceptions came after the Saudi-led coalition, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government, said it had struck Yemen’s Hodeidah .

The Houthi armed group earlier threatened to retaliate against the kingdom’s Red Sea ports, including Jeddah in the event of an attack.

In a statement issued by Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree, the Iran-aligned rebel group urged employees and workers at the ports, as well as people nearby, to evacuate immediately and called on shipping companies to withdraw their vessels.

The attacks are the latest further escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with attacks increasingly targeting strategic infrastructure on both sides.

On Tuesday, a Houthi drone struck the tallest tower in Riyadh, injuring at least 11 people , according to Saudi authorities.

Qatar and Pakistan, which have been mediating efforts to end the wider war in the region between Iran and the United States, both “strongly” condemned the attack on the tower, which houses the Saudi sovereign wealth fund.

The building had already been attacked last Thursday and is one of several high-profile targets hit since fighting with the Iran-backed Yemeni group reignited in July.

The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis promised a firm response to the attack.

The Saudi-led coalition targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah and destroyed several targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada and Amran, al-Maliki said.

Hodeidah, on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, is the main port through which food and other essential supplies enter Houthi-controlled northern Yemen.

It has long served as a key entry point for humanitarian aid and commercial imports, making it a lifeline for millions of Yemenis in a country heavily dependent on imported food.

Renewed fighting between the two sides has intensified since the Houthis announced a blockade on Saudi ports in July. In September, the Iran-aligned group launched a lightning offensive, seizing territory from Yemeni government forces near the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a strategic shipping chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.

Yemeni government forces launched a counteroffensive last month, reclaiming some territory as fighting continues to rage on several fronts.

The Houthis have also stepped up strikes on Saudi airports, ports and oil facilities, while Saudi Arabia has ramped up air strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen in response.

articles.title: A journey to school, marked by play and peril
articles.summary: In South Africa’s Cape Flats, childhood joy is photographed under the shadow of gangs, in Laura Pannack’s new book, “Crossings.”
articles.body: Access to play is a central theme for the young protagonists of Laura Pannack’s new photobook, “Crossings.” Captured primarily outdoors, in neighborhoods across the Cape Flats in South Africa, the children and teenagers in her pictures climb fences and ride their bikes, twist their T-shirts into crop tops and draw chalk shapes on the concrete ground. In one image, a shiny black jacket is draped over the heads of two friends, concealing them from the surrounding world. “That was a really pivotal moment, thinking about the concept of shielding and how these images are read,” said Pannack in a phone call. “Are they shielding from bullets? Are they shielding from me? They’re actually shielding from the sun, the way kids play.” Since residential neighborhoods were first organized as part of the Group Areas Act of 1950 – a piece of apartheid-era legislation that dismantled established communities in urban parts of Cape Town, forcing non-white South Africans onto then largely uninhabited and underdeveloped land – the Cape Flats area has faced poverty, socioeconomic marginalization and escalating gang violence. This heightened inequality and environment of vulnerability remains prevalent today, more than three decades after apartheid ended, and the kids in Pannack’s photos play under the shadow of over 100 competing gangs. Current reports suggest an average of seven people are murdered a day in the Cape Flats. This context informed the direction of “Crossings” said Pannack, who began working on the project while on a residency with A4 Arts Foundation in Cape Town in 2023. The British photographer, whose father was born in South Africa, further explained that the concept, of capturing the journey to and from school, had been percolating for several years prior. “My work has always been about adolescence and those core memories, and the journey to school was kind of imprinted within my mind. I thought it would be an easy framework to produce work that most people can relate to – it’s a rare kind of metaphor for how we evolve and metamorphosize,” she said of the project’s genesis. “It evolved completely with the reality of the situation in South Africa, taking on a totally different, deeper meaning.” Unfolding over three years under the moniker “The Journey Home,” the title “Crossings,” arrived with publisher GOST, and references both the physical journey of moving from one area to another, and the transition from childhood to adulthood. Running workshops with youth clubs, schools and other NGOs in the area until earlier this year, Pannack said making the series was wholly collaborative, and that she was keen to center on the experiences of the participants. “It was very much led by having conversations and listening to the young people talk about their journey to and from school, asking what they see along the way and the fears they have, but also that nostalgic, universal aspect, like the snacks they buy.” “My main objective was not to tell a story I wasn’t part of,” she continued. “There is this huge danger for any artist walking into a foreign space, that you’re speaking for people. That’s why the project took the form it did: I used the money from the residency to run workshops with photography, painting and creative writing, for everyone, regardless of literacy.” Participants ranged in age from four to 19, and the work they produced, including black and white photographs, collages, and cyanotypes, appear in the new book alongside Pannack’s analog color portraits. “They were very open about their experiences,” added the photographer. “No pretense, they were genuinely excited and interested in being creative.” Returning for a month at a time, Pannack was able to build tight relationships with several families, which gave the project a keen sense of intimacy while underscoring the collective sensibility. “I’m always blown away by the imagination and creativity of young people, and by people’s kindness,” she said. “But the level of danger was really eye opening. You hear about it, but to experience it was different. And the way the young people were so used to the violence – and these invisible boundaries of play – really surprised me.” Beyond the workshops, Pannack would accompany kids on their way to and from school, and even snatch time with them during breaktimes on site. “They would usually finish around two or three, but it was so chaotic, some days they just changed the times, or there were days when kids had to go home because of shootings,” she said. “We didn’t see any crossfire, but we were often in a space where the next day or the day before, there was a shooting in that exact spot. One weekend was particularly volatile, eight people were shot and one of them was a kid’s best friend’s dad. Moments like that were a bit of a reality hit. Like wow, these young people are navigating adolescence, and also navigating this situation.” While it’s alluded to, danger is never explicit in “Crossings,” which instead is often filled with smiles, considered poses and playful moments. One site in particular that highlights the sense of community Pannack observed, is a bus stop that features prominently in the book. Pictured both in close-up and from a distance as a kind of monument, the curved structure acts as a safe space for those who gather. “It was just so beautiful, you couldn’t ask for anything better as a backdrop. Hugely graffitied by all the kids, it looked like a work of art for themselves,” said Pannack. “It was the place they loved to hang out, their main base; it was where they behaved completely organically, and it looked great.”

articles.title: Protesters call on Israel to free Palestinian student held without charge
articles.summary: Mahdi Tunsi, 26, was taken from his university dormitory earlier this month and has since been held without charge.
articles.body:
Israeli students, activists and academics are calling for the release of a Palestinian undergraduate who was taken from his university dormitory by Israeli police earlier this month and has since been held without charge.

Mahdi Tunsi, a 26-year-old sociology and criminology student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, appeared in an Israeli court in the city on Tuesday - a hearing that was held behind closed doors.

Israeli police say he was arrested "concerning ties to an act of terrorism".

Authorities have requested what is known as "administrative detention", which allows the Israeli state to detain people indefinitely without charge on the basis of secret evidence that they cannot see.

"We definitely think this is a political arrest," said Dr Yael Berda, one of Tunsi's university professors.

Tunsi, a Palestinian resident of occupied East Jerusalem who works with well-known Jewish-Palestinian campaign groups, was arrested a month after Israel held an election that saw Arab-led parties win a record 19 seats in parliament, the Knesset, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's right-wing coalition lose its majority.

Since then, Berda said she had seen an intensifying campaign against Palestinian rights.

Outside the Jerusalem District Court on Tuesday, demonstrators waved placards with a black-and-white image of Tunsi, while crying out "shame" in unison.

"There's no due process - [administrative detention is] a sugar-coated term for being kidnapped and held as a hostage," said Dr Ofer Cassif, a Member of the Knesset representing the Arab-led Joint List alliance.

"We must all stand firm against such crimes. It's unacceptable."

Since the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, the number of people in administrative detention has more than doubled .

In October, there were more than 3,100 in administrative detention, according to Israel Prison Service figures published by Israeli rights group HaMoked. Most of them are Palestinians from the occupied West Bank.

Israel says that its use of the policy is compliant with international law and a necessary preventative measure to combat terrorism.

In a statement, Israeli police said they would "not elaborate further regarding the investigation" into Tunsi.

He appeared via video link from prison - his hair and beard shaved off. His friends also said that he was without medication as well as his glasses, despite a judge requesting them to be brought to him in detention.

The Israel Prison Service said it acted in accordance with the court's rulings.

"When the process was complete and all the necessary approvals had been received, the detainee's lawyer was told he could pass the eyeglasses to the detainee immediately, subject to security procedures," it added.

Berda asked to enter the courtroom on Tuesday but was denied entry, as was her lawyer. According to Berda, not even Tunsi has been told of the evidence against him.

The judge has said more time is needed to consider the state's request for administrative detention. A decision is expected in the coming days.

"If they have evidence, have them bring it or release him," said Berda.

"That's why we're demanding his immediate release or moving it to a criminal track where he could defend himself."

Berda said that while Tunsi could not vote in Israel's general election because he is not an Israeli citizen, he was "engaged" and very supportive of Arab parties' involvement.

"Mahdi is one of the best human beings I know," said Noga Kaplan, who studies with him at the Hebrew University.

"He has a really pure heart and is very passionate about his studies."

After Tunsi's arrest, the Hebrew University issued a statement saying it was notified a few minutes before it took place.

"The university is not a party to the legal proceedings involving the student, and we do not have information that would allow us to comment on the circumstances leading to the arrest or on the ongoing legal proceedings," it said.

It added that it was concerned for Tunsi's well-being and hoped "that the matter will be resolved promptly and that his rights will be fully respected throughout the process".

Tunsi is a resident of Silwan, a neighbourhood in East Jerusalem where, in recent years, Palestinians have been evicted by Israeli authorities , who say their properties were built illegally. Israeli settlers have since moved into some of those properties.

"Political organisation stopped after October 7 because people were getting super scared about the consequences," explained Kaplan.

"Mahdi saw studying as one of the ways to speak about it in class."

"He didn't do a lot of public stuff because what's happening now is his biggest fear."

articles.title: Who is Chen Jining, China’s latest Politburo member under investigation?
articles.summary: Chen is the fourth high-ranking Politburo member to be pushed out in two years.
articles.body:
The Chinese Communist Party has launched investigations into the party’s Shanghai secretary Chen Jining for alleged “serious violations of discipline and law” – usually code for corruption.

The anticorruption watchdog, the Central Commission for Discipline Inspection, announced the probe in a brief statement on Tuesday, according to Xinhua News Agency, but did not give more details.

It comes amid widespread purges in the Political Bureau, one of the top bodies of the CCP, as the party prepares for its next congress in the second half of 2027, where President Xi Jinping is expected to clinch his fourth five-year term.

Xi, who has pushed greater party discipline and anticorruption, has for years pursued a long, intense purge on a scale not seen since the rule of Mao Zedong, experts say.

Chen is the fourth high-ranking Politburo member to be pushed out in two years.

The Shanghai Communist Party’s leaders have backed the move, with its standing committee stating it firmly supported the decision to investigate Chen and that it showed Beijing’s determination to continue its anticorruption campaign.

“The takedown again shows that Xi Jinping’s anticorruption campaign has no limits,” Mingda Qiu, a senior analyst at Eurasia Group, told The Associated Press news agency. “The pattern is unprecedented.” Here’s what we know:

Chen, 62, joined the CCP as a 20-year-old environmental engineering student at the highly-rated Tsinghua University. After spending a decade researching in the United Kingdom, the scientist and academic returned to Tsinghua, where he was eventually appointed one of its youngest presidents in 2012.

He went on to serve as the Minister of Environmental Protection from 2015 to 2017, and led efforts to cut pollution in Beijing. He was later appointed Mayor of Beijing in 2018.

In 2022, he was appointed party secretary of Shanghai, the country’s financial hub, amid Xi’s push to install people with strong scientific backgrounds in key roles.

Chen was widely seen as Xi’s protege. His post is usually seen as a stepping stone to party leadership; President Xi previously held the position of Shanghai Party Secretary in 2007.

Chen hosted some of China’s most prominent diplomatic visitors, including former US Secretary of State Antony Blinken, former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni.

He led the opening ceremony of the World AI Conference held earlier this year in Shanghai.

Other senior party officials have been purged in recent months, especially in the military.

General Zhang Youxia , the senior vice chair of the powerful Central Military Commission (CMC), was investigated for the same “serious violations of discipline and law”, China’s Defence Ministry said in January. The commission is the top military body and is chaired by Xi, making Zhang the military’s number two. He was part of the informal “Shaanxi clique”, a network of political leaders who share ancestral ties to Shaanxi Province with Xi.

Liu Zhenli, another CMC member who served as the chief of staff of its Joint Staff Department, was being investigated by the CCP, the Defence Ministry also said in January.

He Weidong, the other vice chair of the military commission, was expelled last October on allegations of “serious misconduct” and violations involving “exceptionally large amounts of money”. Eight other senior military members were also dismissed. He was part of the “Fujian clique”, a tight circle of officials who have long been allied with President Xi since his time as Fujian governor from 1999.

Miao Hua, former head of the political work department in the military commission and another member of the Fujian clique, was removed in June 2025.

Ma Xingrui, former party secretary of Xinjiang, was charged with accepting “exceptionally large” bribes in November. Ma’s investigation was first announced in April.

The military shakeups and wider purge are part of Xi’s years-long anticorruption drive that has seen hundreds of senior and junior government officials investigated, prosecuted or dismissed since Xi first came to power in 2012.

Analysts believe the purges are designed to reform the military and to ensure unwavering loyalty to Xi.

Some military expulsions have been linked to suspicions of political divergence. Official sources, for example, described additional allegations against He Weidong, the former vice chairman of the military commission, as being a “loss of chastity,” a rare phrase which, in CCP speak, refers to political disloyalty and ideological collapse.

The takedowns reveal how Chinese politics often depends on shifting circumstances, with even officials possessing the qualifications Xi wants being vulnerable to removal, said Joseph Torigian, a professor at the Washington-based American University.

“On paper,” they appear to be “individuals Xi would appreciate,” Torigian told the AP. But afterwards, “we could easily come up with hypotheses for why he got rid of them”.
